title: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget.
ballot_label: Caption: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city’s annual discretionary budget. Question: Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city’s discretionary budget?
summary: A citizen-initiated Portland charter amendment requiring the City Council to allocate an amount equal to at least 2% of the city's adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses to a participatory budgeting program. Residents could propose citywide or district projects; city staff and budget delegates would refine proposals, and residents would make binding selections. An oversight committee of residents would help develop the program, which would start July 2027.
yes_means: A yes vote amends the Portland City Charter to create a participatory budgeting program in which residents make binding decisions on spending an amount equal to at least 2% of the city's discretionary budget.
no_means: A no vote leaves the current budget process unchanged, in which the Mayor proposes and the Council amends and adopts the budget.
fiscal_impact: Under a recent forecast, the ballot summary gives a preliminary estimate of $16.4 million in FY 2027-28 and $17.0 million in FY 2028-29 to be allocated to the program; Council may identify funding from the entire city budget to meet the obligation.

arguments.author: Devin Ruiz, deputy director, NextUp Action Fund
arguments.statement: Devin Ruiz of NextUp Action Fund, which helped fund the measure's committee, says the measure gives Portlanders a direct way to push back on cuts and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.
arguments.excerpt: Your 2 Cents gives Portlanders a direct way to push back and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.

arguments.author: Jim Labbe, chief petitioner; executive director, Participatory Budgeting Oregon
arguments.statement: Chief petitioner Jim Labbe says Portland has a public trust crisis about how it spends money and that participatory budgeting is a demonstrated bottom-up mechanism to address it.
arguments.excerpt: It's got to be from the bottom up, and participatory budgeting is really a demonstrated mechanism to do that.

arguments.author: Jim Labbe, chief petitioner; executive director, Participatory Budgeting Oregon
arguments.statement: Labbe says a recurring process in which residents register priorities and create data to inform the budget is the missing piece.
arguments.excerpt: "Having a recurring process in which residents can register their priorities and create data to inform the budget," Labbe said. "That's the missing piece."

arguments.author: Mayor Keith Wilson
arguments.statement: Mayor Keith Wilson says the measure would write a permanent budget set-aside into the charter that no future mayor or council could adjust.
arguments.excerpt: No future mayor or council could adjust it.

arguments.author: Mayor Keith Wilson
arguments.statement: Wilson says the measure would take at least $16 million a year from the fund that pays for shelter beds, park maintenance and investigators, and that Portland cannot afford it.
arguments.excerpt: Wilson said in a statement the measure would pull “at least $16 million a year from the fund that pays for shelter beds, park maintenance, and investigators, and [hand] it to a process the measure doesn’t even define,” something “Portland can’t afford,” he wrote.

arguments.author: Laurie Wimmer, executive secretary-treasurer, Northwest Oregon Labor Council; chair, Protect Our City Services PAC
arguments.statement: Laurie Wimmer, who chairs the opposing committee Protect Our City Services, says the measure would take millions from parks, community centers, Portland Street Response, firefighting and other services.
arguments.excerpt: take millions away from parks, community centers, Portland Street Response, firefighting, and other essential services
